guided_journeys.story_title: The Archive That Could Not Make a Copy
guided_journeys.tagline: One tagged DNA molecule has been cleared as hereditary information, but the replication works will not certify a copy until its chromosome form, base geometry, replication model, directional machinery, repair, and chromosome ends all agree.

guide.name: Dr. Sora Han
guide.visual: dark-cobalt lab coat, clear gloves, transparent 5′→3′ compass tablet, and a narrow copper information ledger
guide.story_job: Sora keeps the same blue-and-gold DNA duplex, its original strand identities, and every 5′/3′ direction marker visible as the molecule moves from storage into replication. She points to real biological structures, changes only the feature needed for the mechanism, and names terms after their defining action is visible.

guided_journeys.premise: The Genome Archive has received a blue-and-gold DNA molecule for long-term hereditary storage, yet the attached replication works refuse to copy it. The archive records disagree about chromosome form, extra-chromosomal plasmids are mixed with the main chromosome, base classes are being confused with pairing partners, and the copying machinery has lost the strand directions that determine how replication can proceed. Dr. Sora Han must carry the same tagged duplex through the archive and replication works, resolving each physical inconsistency before the next machine can activate.
guided_journeys.mission: Follow Dr. Sora Han through twelve connected locations. Keep the same parental DNA strands, 5′/3′ arrows, and copper origin tag visible from the hereditary-information registry through semiconservative replication, fork opening, primer-dependent synthesis, leading/lagging geometry, fragment joining, repair, and chromosome-end maintenance.
guided_journeys.finale: The archive certifies two semiconservative daughter DNA molecules only after every step remains physically consistent with the original molecule. One parental strand persists in each daughter duplex, all new DNA was synthesized 5′→3′, the lagging strand was completed and repaired, and telomeres remain chromosome-end DNA distinct from telomerase. The same DNA information can now leave the copying works and enter the later RNA-expression route without losing its molecular history.

guided_journeys.story_title: The Message That Was Not Ready to Leave
guided_journeys.tagline: One tagged gene has been cleared for expression, but the workshop cannot release its RNA until RNA roles, template choice, promoter entry, transcription direction, cellular context, end processing, and splicing all agree.

guide.name: Dr. Sora Han
guide.visual: dark-cobalt lab coat, clear gloves, transparent 5′→3′ compass tablet, and a narrow copper information ledger
guide.story_job: Sora keeps the same tagged gene, violet template strand, promoter marker, and growing RNA transcript visible from the first RNA desk through transcription and RNA processing. She points to real molecules, changes only the feature needed for the mechanism, and names terms after their defining action is visible.

guided_journeys.premise: A tagged gene arrives at the RNA Transcript Workshop with its violet template strand marked and a blank red transcript ribbon clipped beside it. The workshop has mixed mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA into one generic RNA category, lost the distinction between transcription and translation, and routed both bacterial and eukaryotic transcripts through the same exit. Dr. Sora Han must follow one gene and its RNA product through eight connected locations, preserving strand direction and cellular context while the message is made and, where appropriate, processed.
guided_journeys.mission: Follow the tagged gene from RNA-role sorting through transcription entry and directional synthesis, then compare the open prokaryotic exit with the eukaryotic pre-mRNA processing route. Keep the same violet template strand and red RNA transcript identifiable while promoter, 5′→3′ synthesis, cap, poly-A tail, introns, exons, alternative splicing, and mature mRNA are resolved.
guided_journeys.finale: The workshop releases a mature eukaryotic mRNA only after the same transcript has been synthesized 5′→3′ from one DNA template, distinguished from bacterial transcript handling, capped, polyadenylated, and spliced. The tagged gene remains DNA, transcription remains distinct from translation, and the completed red RNA message exits toward the ribosome with its processing history reconstructable from the route.

guided_journeys.story_title: The Assembly Line That Lost Its Reading Frame
guided_journeys.tagline: A mature mRNA has reached the hall intact, but no protein can be built until the start position, codon code, charged tRNAs, ribosome traffic, elongation cycle, and stop logic all agree.

guide.name: Dr. Sora Han
guide.visual: dark-cobalt lab coat, clear gloves, transparent 5′→3′ compass tablet, and a narrow copper information ledger
guide.story_job: Sora keeps the same mature red mRNA ribbon, highlighted AUG start codon, fixed triplet spacing, and growing polypeptide visible through the entire translation route. She points to real ribosomes, tRNAs, codons, amino acids, and enzymes and names terms only after their defining structure or action is visible.

guided_journeys.premise: The mature red mRNA from the previous journey arrives at the Translation Assembly Hall with its sequence intact, AUG highlighted, and triplet spacing visible, yet the assembly line has lost the rules that turn the message into an ordered polypeptide. Ribosomes have been routed without regard to cellular geography, the reading frame can slide, tRNAs are arriving unloaded, the A/P/E positions are mixed together, and the stop signal is being treated as though it should recruit another amino acid. Dr. Sora Han must keep the same mRNA and one growing polypeptide identifiable while each part of translation is restored in causal order.
guided_journeys.mission: Carry one mature mRNA from the correct cellular translation site through start-codon recognition, reading-frame locking, codon interpretation, tRNA charging and delivery, ribosomal A/P/E organization, repeated elongation, and termination. Preserve the same mRNA sequence and triplet spacing while the polypeptide grows only when the ribosome advances by one codon, then keep retroviral reverse transcription physically separate as an RNA-to-DNA information-flow case rather than confusing it with ordinary translation.
guided_journeys.finale: The ribosome reaches a stop codon without inventing a stop amino acid, termination machinery releases the completed polypeptide, and the chain continues folding while the original mRNA remains intact. Through a separate side gate, retroviral RNA is copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase and routed toward host-genome integration. The learner can reconstruct both routes from real molecular direction and function, with the ordinary translation pathway preserved from mature mRNA to amino-acid sequence.

guided_journeys.story_title: The Control Center That Forgot Its Cell Identities
guided_journeys.tagline: The genome has not changed, but every cell is drifting toward the same output state. Follow one tracked gene through bacterial comparison switches and the layered eukaryotic control system until distinct expression profiles and specialized cell identities can be restored.

guide.name: Dr. Sora Han
guide.visual: dark-cobalt lab coat, clear gloves, transparent 5′→3′ compass tablet, and a narrow copper information ledger
guide.story_job: Sora keeps one tracked eukaryotic gene, its promoter-linked expression meter, and its chromatin-state strip identifiable through the regulation route. She uses separate bacterial operon models for trp and lac comparisons so those systems never become confused with the tracked eukaryotic gene.

guided_journeys.premise: A gene-control failure has flattened expression across a bank of model cells. The cells still carry matching genomes, yet regulatory outputs that should differ by condition, cell type, and developmental state are converging toward the same pattern. Dr. Sora Han seals one tracked eukaryotic gene sequence so it cannot change and attaches an expression meter and chromatin-state strip. To restore cell identity, you must determine how gene output can change around an unchanged sequence. The route first descends through two bacterial operon comparison chambers, then returns to the tracked eukaryotic gene and follows regulation through chromatin, transcriptional recruitment, negative regulation, RNA-level control, expression profiles, differentiation, and developmental sequencing.
guided_journeys.mission: Keep the tracked gene sequence fixed while changing only the scientifically relevant control layer. Distinguish constitutive from inducible expression, operon DNA from repressor protein, repressible trp logic from inducible lac logic, and bacterial control from eukaryotic layered regulation. Then follow the same eukaryotic gene through reversible epigenetic state, promoter/enhancer recruitment, negative transcriptional regulation, RNA-level control, multigene expression profiles, cell specialization, and developmental gene-expression sequences. At every stage, identify which molecule or regulatory state changed and which output changed as a consequence.
guided_journeys.finale: The final developmental hall restores distinct cell identities without altering the tracked genome. Cytoplasmic determinants and inductive signals alter developmental gene expression, transcription factors act in sequence, regional patterning and homeotic-gene logic contribute to positional identity, morphogenesis changes tissue form, and apoptosis removes selected cells during normal remodeling. Looking back through the center, the learner can reconstruct a single causal principle across very different mechanisms. Stable DNA sequence does not imply fixed gene output. Regulatory DNA, regulatory proteins, chromatin, RNA processing and stability, translation, protein state, developmental signals, and expression profiles can all change what a cell produces and therefore what the cell becomes.

guided_journeys.story_title: The Mutation Yard Where Every Change Was Blamed
guided_journeys.tagline: A forensic yard has stamped every genetic difference as a harmful mutation. Keep one reference genome visible while you classify substitutions, frameshifts, chromosome errors, horizontal transfer, transposition, and viral recombination by what physically changed and what consequence actually followed.

guide.name: Dr. Sora Han
guide.visual: dark-cobalt lab coat, clear gloves, transparent 5′→3′ compass tablet, and a narrow copper information ledger
guide.story_job: Sora keeps one blue reference DNA/chromosome state and one amber altered or acquired state identifiable across the mutation yard. She requires every case to be classified by what physically changed first, then by molecular consequence, phenotype, environment, or transfer route.

guided_journeys.premise: An automated triage system has collapsed every kind of genetic difference into one red HARMFUL MUTATION label. A one-base substitution, an altered reading frame, a chromosome-number error, a rearranged chromosome, horizontally acquired DNA, a transposable element, and viral recombination are being treated as if they were the same mechanism with the same consequence. Dr. Sora Han locks one blue reference genome onto her copper ledger and tags every altered or acquired state amber. The only way to clear the yard is to classify each case from physical evidence before interpreting phenotype or evolutionary significance.
guided_journeys.mission: Keep the blue reference DNA or chromosome state visible at every locus. First identify whether the case changes a nucleotide, reading frame, chromosome number, chromosome structure, DNA-transfer route, mobile-element position, or viral sequence combination. Then trace molecular product, phenotype, environmental context, inheritance, or selection only when scientifically warranted. Distinguish silent, missense, and nonsense substitutions; distinguish frameshift from every insertion/deletion; distinguish nondisjunction from structural rearrangement; and distinguish transformation, transduction, conjugation, transposition, and viral recombination by mechanism.
guided_journeys.finale: The final yard removes the universal HARMFUL stamp and replaces it with a mechanism-and-consequence report. The learner can reconstruct how mutations can have neutral, detrimental, or beneficial effects depending on molecular and environmental context; how mutation creates novel sequence variation while reproduction reshuffles variation; how chromosome-number and chromosome-structure changes differ; how horizontal gene transfer moves DNA outside parent-to-offspring inheritance; and how transposition and viral recombination generate distinct forms of genomic variation.
